passage:
Most schools today allow students to carry smartphones, and many teenagers spend several hours a day on social media platforms. Governments and school boards have started debating whether social media use should be restricted for young people during school hours — or even banned altogether for those under a certain age. The debate has grown louder as more studies link heavy social media use to anxiety, poor sleep, and declining attention spans in adolescents.

Paul Mercer is the spokesperson for the Digital Literacy Council, a group backed by major technology companies. "Banning social media for teenagers is an overreaction," he says. "Young people are going to enter a world where digital communication is everywhere. Schools should be teaching them how to use these tools responsibly, not shutting them out entirely. Blocking access does not build skills — it just delays an inevitable conversation."

Mercer also warns that heavy-handed restrictions create other problems. "When you ban something outright, you drive it underground. Teenagers will simply find ways around the rules, and without proper guidance, they will be even less equipped to handle what they find online. Regulation without education is a recipe for disaster."

Dr. Fatima Syed, a child psychologist with the Youth Wellbeing Institute, strongly disagrees. "The evidence is clear — excessive social media use is damaging young people's mental health. We are not talking about occasional use; we are talking about compulsive scrolling that interrupts sleep, fuels social comparison, and displaces real-world relationships. Restricting access during school hours is the bare minimum. Many countries have already moved to ban social media for those under sixteen, and the results have been encouraging."

Dr. Syed also dismisses the argument that bans reduce digital literacy. "Learning to drive safely does not mean letting a twelve-year-old loose on a motorway. Children need boundaries. Responsible digital habits are built through structure and guidance — not through unlimited, unsupervised access at an age when the brain is still developing."
